1 INTRODUCTION: Mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) is a type of optimization problems that minimize a linear objective function subject to linear constraints, where some or all variables must take integer values. MILP has a wide type of applications, such as transportation Schouwenaars et al. (2001), control Richards & How (2005), scheduling Floudas & Lin (2005), etc. Branch and Bound (B&B) Land & Doig (1960), an algorithm widely adopted in modern solvers that exactly solves general MILPs to global optimality, unfortunately, has an exponential time complexity in the worst-case sense. To make MILP more practical, researchers have to analyze the features of each instance of interest based on their domain knowledge, and use such features to adaptively warm-start B&B or design the heuristics in B&B. To automate such laborious process, researchers turn attention to Machine learning (ML) techniques in recent years Bengio et al. (2021). The literature has reported some encouraging findings that a proper chosen ML model is able to learn some useful knowledge of MILP from data and generalize well to some similar but unseen instances. For example, one can learn fast approximations of Strong Branching, an effective but time-consuming branching strategy usually used in B&B Alvarez et al. (2014); Khalil et al. (2016); Zarpellon et al. (2021); Lin et al. (2022). One may also learn cutting strategies Tang et al. (2020); Berthold et al. (2022); Huang et al. (2022), node selection/pruning strategies He et al. (2014); Yilmaz & Yorke-Smith (2020), or decomposition strategies Song et al. (2020) with ML models. The role of ML models in those approaches can be summarized as: approximating useful mappings or parameterizing key strategies in MILP solvers, and these mappings/strategies usually take an MILP instance as input and output its key peroperties. The graph neural network (GNN), due to its nice properties, say permutation invariance, is considered a suitable model to represent such mappings/strategies for MILP. More specifically, permutations on variables or constraints of an MILP do not essentially change the problem itself, reliable ML models such as GNNs should satisfy such properties, otherwise the model may overfit to the variable/constraint orders in the training data. Gasse et al. (2019) proposed that an MILP can be encoded into a bipartite graph on which one can use a GNN to approximate Strong Branching. Ding et al. (2020) proposed to represent MILP with a tripartite graph. Since then, GNNs have been adopted to represent mappings/strategies for MILP, for example, approximating Strong Branching Gupta et al. (2020); Nair et al. (2020); Shen et al. (2021); Gupta et al. (2022), approximating optimal so- lution Nair et al. (2020); Khalil et al. (2022), parameterizing cutting strategies Paulus et al. (2022), and parameterizing branching strategies Qu et al. (2022); Scavuzzo et al. (2022). However, theoretical foundations in this direction still remain unclear. A key problem is the ability of GNN to approximate important mappings related with MILP. In this paper, we ask the following questions: Is GNN able to predict whether an MILP is feasible? (Q1) Is GNN able to approximate the optimal objective value of an MILP? (Q2) Is GNN able to approximate an optimal solution of an MILP? (Q3) To answer questions (Q1 - Q3), one needs theories of separation power and representation power of GNN. The separation power of GNN is measured by whether it can distinguish two non-isomorphic graphs. Given two graphs G1, G2, we say a mapping F (e.g. a GNN) has strong separation power if F (G1) ̸= F (G2) as long as G1, G2 that are not the isomorphic. In our settings, since MILPs are represented by graphs, the separation power actually indicates the ability of GNN to distinguish two different MILP instances. The representation power of GNN refers to how well it can approximate mappings with permutation invariant properties. In our settings, we study whether GNN can map an MILP to its feasiblity, optimal objective value and an optimal solution. The separation power and representation power of GNNs are closely related to the WeisfeilerLehman (WL) test Weisfeiler & Leman (1968), a classical algorithm to identify whether two graphs are isomorphic or not. In the literature, it has been shown that GNN has the same separation power with the WL test Xu et al. (2019), and, based on this result, GNNs can universally approximate continuous graph-input mappings with separation power no stronger than WL test Azizian & Lelarge (2021); Geerts & Reutter (2022). Our contributions With the above tools in hand, one still cannot directly answer questions (Q1 - Q3) since the relationship between characteristics of general MILPs and properties of graphs are not clear yet. Although there are some works studying the representation power of GNN on some graphrelated optimization problems Sato et al. (2019); Loukas (2020) and linear programming Chen et al. (2022), representing general MILPs with GNNs are still not theoretically studied, to the best of our knowledge. Our contributions are listed below: • (Limitation of GNNs for MILP) We show with an example that GNNs do not have strong enough separation power to distinguish any two different MILP instances. There exist two MILPs such that one of them is feasible while the other one is not, but, unfortunately, all GNNs treat them equally without detecting the essential difference between them. In fact, there are infinitely many pairs of MILP instances that can puzzle GNN. • (Foldable and unfoldable MILP) We provide a precise mathematical description on what type of MILPs makes GNNs fail. These hard MILP instances are named as foldable MILPs. We prove that, after restricting dataset to unfoldable MILPs, GNN has strong enough separation power and representation power to approximate the feasibility, optimal objective value and an optimal solution of an MILP. • (MILP with random features) To handle those foldable MILPs, we propose to append random features to the MILP-induced graphs. We prove that, with the random feature technique, the answers to questions (Q1 - Q3) are affirmative. The rest of this paper is organized as follows. We state some preliminaries in Section 2. The limitation of GNN for MILP is presented in Section 3 and we provide the descriptions of foldable and unfoldable MILPs in Section 4. The random feature technique is introduced in Section 5. Review the following paper for International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR) 2023. Remember you need to make 3 reviewer agents for each paper. GIVE A FINAL DECISION in the form of "FINAL DECISION: <Accept/Reject>". The paper title is: On Representing Mixed-Integer Linear Programs by Graph Neural Networks

1 INTRODUCTION: Mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) is a type of optimization problems that minimize a linear objective function subject to linear constraints, where some or all variables must take integer values. MILP has a wide type of applications, such as transportation Schouwenaars et al. (2001), control Richards & How (2005), scheduling Floudas & Lin (2005), etc. Branch and Bound (B&B) Land & Doig (1960), an algorithm widely adopted in modern solvers that exactly solves general MILPs to global optimality, unfortunately, has an exponential time complexity in the worst-case sense. To make MILP more practical, researchers have to analyze the features of each instance of interest based on their domain knowledge, and use such features to adaptively warm-start B&B or design the heuristics in B&B. To automate such laborious process, researchers turn attention to Machine learning (ML) techniques in recent years Bengio et al. (2021). The literature has reported some encouraging findings that a proper chosen ML model is able to learn some useful knowledge of MILP from data and generalize well to some similar but unseen instances. For example, one can learn fast approximations of Strong Branching, an effective but time-consuming branching strategy usually used in B&B Alvarez et al. (2014); Khalil et al. (2016); Zarpellon et al. (2021); Lin et al. (2022). One may also learn cutting strategies Tang et al. (2020); Berthold et al. (2022); Huang et al. (2022), node selection/pruning strategies He et al. (2014); Yilmaz & Yorke-Smith (2020), or decomposition strategies Song et al. (2020) with ML models. The role of ML models in those approaches can be summarized as: approximating useful mappings or parameterizing key strategies in MILP solvers, and these mappings/strategies usually take an MILP instance as input and output its key peroperties. The graph neural network (GNN), due to its nice properties, say permutation invariance, is considered a suitable model to represent such mappings/strategies for MILP. More specifically, permutations on variables or constraints of an MILP do not essentially change the problem itself, reliable ML models such as GNNs should satisfy such properties, otherwise the model may overfit to the variable/constraint orders in the training data. Gasse et al. (2019) proposed that an MILP can be encoded into a bipartite graph on which one can use a GNN to approximate Strong Branching. Ding et al. (2020) proposed to represent MILP with a tripartite graph. Since then, GNNs have been adopted to represent mappings/strategies for MILP, for example, approximating Strong Branching Gupta et al. (2020); Nair et al. (2020); Shen et al. (2021); Gupta et al. (2022), approximating optimal so- lution Nair et al. (2020); Khalil et al. (2022), parameterizing cutting strategies Paulus et al. (2022), and parameterizing branching strategies Qu et al. (2022); Scavuzzo et al. (2022). However, theoretical foundations in this direction still remain unclear. A key problem is the ability of GNN to approximate important mappings related with MILP. In this paper, we ask the following questions: Is GNN able to predict whether an MILP is feasible? (Q1) Is GNN able to approximate the optimal objective value of an MILP? (Q2) Is GNN able to approximate an optimal solution of an MILP? (Q3) To answer questions (Q1 - Q3), one needs theories of separation power and representation power of GNN. The separation power of GNN is measured by whether it can distinguish two non-isomorphic graphs. Given two graphs G1, G2, we say a mapping F (e.g. a GNN) has strong separation power if F (G1) ̸= F (G2) as long as G1, G2 that are not the isomorphic. In our settings, since MILPs are represented by graphs, the separation power actually indicates the ability of GNN to distinguish two different MILP instances. The representation power of GNN refers to how well it can approximate mappings with permutation invariant properties. In our settings, we study whether GNN can map an MILP to its feasiblity, optimal objective value and an optimal solution. The separation power and representation power of GNNs are closely related to the WeisfeilerLehman (WL) test Weisfeiler & Leman (1968), a classical algorithm to identify whether two graphs are isomorphic or not. In the literature, it has been shown that GNN has the same separation power with the WL test Xu et al. (2019), and, based on this result, GNNs can universally approximate continuous graph-input mappings with separation power no stronger than WL test Azizian & Lelarge (2021); Geerts & Reutter (2022). Our contributions With the above tools in hand, one still cannot directly answer questions (Q1 - Q3) since the relationship between characteristics of general MILPs and properties of graphs are not clear yet. Although there are some works studying the representation power of GNN on some graphrelated optimization problems Sato et al. (2019); Loukas (2020) and linear programming Chen et al. (2022), representing general MILPs with GNNs are still not theoretically studied, to the best of our knowledge. Our contributions are listed below: • (Limitation of GNNs for MILP) We show with an example that GNNs do not have strong enough separation power to distinguish any two different MILP instances. There exist two MILPs such that one of them is feasible while the other one is not, but, unfortunately, all GNNs treat them equally without detecting the essential difference between them. In fact, there are infinitely many pairs of MILP instances that can puzzle GNN. • (Foldable and unfoldable MILP) We provide a precise mathematical description on what type of MILPs makes GNNs fail. These hard MILP instances are named as foldable MILPs. We prove that, after restricting dataset to unfoldable MILPs, GNN has strong enough separation power and representation power to approximate the feasibility, optimal objective value and an optimal solution of an MILP. • (MILP with random features) To handle those foldable MILPs, we propose to append random features to the MILP-induced graphs. We prove that, with the random feature technique, the answers to questions (Q1 - Q3) are affirmative. The rest of this paper is organized as follows. We state some preliminaries in Section 2. The limitation of GNN for MILP is presented in Section 3 and we provide the descriptions of foldable and unfoldable MILPs in Section 4. The random feature technique is introduced in Section 5. Section 6 contains some numerical results and the whole paper is concluded in Section 7. 2 PRELIMINARIES: In this section, we introduce some preliminaries that will be used throughout this paper. Our notations and definitions follow Chen et al. (2022). Consider a general MILP problem defined with: min x∈Rn c⊤x, s.t. Ax ◦ b, l ≤ x ≤ u, xj ∈ Z, ∀ j ∈ NI , (2.1) where A ∈ Rm×n, c ∈ Rn, b ∈ Rm, l ∈ (R ∪ {−∞})n, u ∈ (R ∪ {+∞})n, and ◦ ∈ {≤,=,≥}m. The index set NI ⊂ {1, 2, . . . , n} includes those indices j where xj are constrained to be an integer. The feasible set is defined with Xfeasible := {x ∈ Rn|Ax ◦ b, l ≤ x ≤ u, xj ∈ Z,∀ j ∈ NI}, and we say an MILP is infeasible if Xfeasible = ∅ and feasible otherwise. For feasible MILPs, inf{c⊤x : x ∈ Xfeasible} is named as the optimal objective value. If there exists x∗ ∈ Xfeasible with c⊤x∗ ≤ c⊤x, ∀ x ∈ Xfeasible, then we say that x∗ is an optimal solution. It is possible that the objective value is arbitrarily good, i.e., for any R > 0, c⊤x̂ < −R holds for some x̂ ∈ Xfeasible. In this case, we say the MILP is unbounded or its optimal objective value is −∞. 2.1 MILP AS A WEIGHTED BIPARTITE GRAPH WITH VERTEX FEATURES: All information in an MILP (2.1) can be represented into a weighted bipartite graph. The vertex set of such a graph is V ∪W , where V = {v1, v2, . . . , vm} with vi corresponding to the i-th constraint, and W = {w1, w2, . . . , wm} with wj corresponding to the j-th variable. The edge Ei,j ∈ R connects vi ∈ V and wj ∈ W , and Ei,j = 0 if there is no connection between vi and wj . Note that there is no edge connecting vertices in the same vertex group (V or W ). Thus, the whole graph is denoted as G = (V ∪ W,E), and we denote Gm,n as the collection of all such weighted bipartite graphs whose two vertex groups have size m and n, respectively. To fully represent all information in (2.1), we associate each vertex in V ∪W with vertex features: • The vertex vi ∈ V represents the i-th constraint in (2.1), and it is equipped with a feature vector hVi = (bi, ◦i) that is in the space HV = R× {≤,=,≥}. • The vertex wj ∈ W represents the j-th variable in (2.1), and it is equipped with a feature vector hWj = (cj , lj , uj , τj), where τj = 1 if j ∈ NI and τj = 0 otherwise. The feature hWj is in the space HW = R× (R ∪ {−∞})× (R ∪ {+∞})× {0, 1}. • The edge Ei,j connects the i-th constraint and the j-th variable in (2.1) with the weight being Ei,j = Ai,j . Finally, we define HVm := (HV )m and HWn := (HW )n, and stack all the vertex features together as H = (hV1 , h V 2 , . . . , h V m, h W 1 , h W 2 , . . . , h W n ) ∈ HVm ×HWn . Then a weighted bipartite graph with vertex features (G,H) ∈ Gm,n × HVm × HWn contains all information in the MILP problem (2.1). This approach to represent a general MILP with a graph is first introduced in Gasse et al. (2019), and in this paper, we call the resulting graph as an MILP-induced graph or MILP-graph. If NI = ∅, the feature τj can be dropped and the graphs reduce to LP-graphs in Chen et al. (2022). We provide an example of MILP-graph in Figure 1. 2.2 GRAPH NEURAL NETWORKS WITH MESSAGE PASSING FOR MILP-GRAPHS: To represent properties of the whole graph, one needs to build a GNN that maps (G,H) to a real number: Gm,n×HVm×HWn → R; to represent properties of each vertex in W (or represent properties for each variable), one needs to build a GNN that maps (G,H) to a vector: Gm,n×HVm×HWn → Rn. In this section, we explicitly describe the GNNs used in this paper. The first step in the construction of GNNs is the embedding step. Let fVin : HV → Rd0 and fWin : HW → Rd0 be learnable functions that embed the vertex features, hVi and hWj , into initial hidden states h0,Vi , h 0,W j ∈ Rd0 : h0,Vi = f V in (h V i ), h 0,W j = f W in (h W j ), i = 1, 2, . . . ,m, j = 1, 2, . . . , n, (2.2) Then {h0,Vi }mi=0 and {h 0,W j }nj=0 are updated layer by layer via local updates as well as message passing. Let L be the number of message-passing layers. For 1 ≤ l ≤ L, the hidden states at the l-th layer, hl,Vi , h l,W j ∈ Rdl , can be computed from the the hidden states at the (l − 1)-th layer via learnable functions fVl , f W l : Rdl−1 → Rdl and gVl , gWl : Rdl−1 × Rdl → Rdl : hl,Vi = g V l ( hl−1,Vi , n∑ j=1 Ei,jf W l (h l−1,W j ) ) , i = 1, 2, . . . ,m, (2.3) hl,Wj = g W l ( hl−1,Wj , m∑ i=1 Ei,jf V l (h l−1,V i ) ) , j = 1, 2, . . . , n. (2.4) The output layer differs for scalar-output GNNs and vertex-output GNNs. The scalar output can be defined by: yout = fout ( m∑ i=1 hL,Vi , n∑ j=1 hL,Wj ) , (2.5) where fout : RdL × RdL → R is some learnable function. For vertex-output GNNs, the output for vertex wj ∈ W is given by yout(wi) = f W out ( m∑ i=1 hL,Vi , n∑ j=1 hL,Wj , h L,W i ) , i = 1, 2, · · · , n, (2.6) where fWout : RdL × RdL × RdL → R is a learnable function. Throughout this paper, we require all learnable functions to be continuous following the same settings as in Chen et al. (2022); Azizian & Lelarge (2021), and we denote FGNN and FWGNN as the function classes for the two types of GNNs. Particularly, we define FGNN :={F : Gm,n ×HVm ×HWn → R | F yields (2.2), (2.3), (2.4), (2.5)}, FWGNN :={F : Gm,n ×HVm ×HWn → Rn | F yields (2.2), (2.3), (2.4), (2.6)}. (2.7) 2.3 MAPPINGS TO REPRESENT MILP CHARACTERISTICS: Now we introduce the mappings that are what we aim to approximate by GNNs. With the definitions, we will revisit questions (Q1-Q3) and describe them in a mathematically precise way. Feasibility mapping We first define the following mapping that indicates the feasibility of MILP: Φfeas : Gm,n ×HVm ×HWn → {0, 1}, where Φfeas(G,H) = 1 if (G,H) corresponds to a feasible MILP and Φfeas(G,H) = 0 otherwise. Optimal objective value mapping We then define the following mapping that maps an MILP to its optimal objective value: Φobj : Gm,n ×HVm ×HWn → R ∪ {∞,−∞}, where Φobj(G,H) = ∞ implies infeasibility and Φobj(G,H) = −∞ implies unboundedness. Note that the optimal objective value for MILP may be an infimum that can never be achieved. An example would be minx∈Z2 x1 + πx2, s.t. x1 + πx2 ≥ √ 2. The optimal objective value is √ 2, since for any ϵ > 0, there exists a feasible x with x1 + πx2 < √ 2 + ϵ. However, there is no x ∈ Z2 such that x1+πx2 = √ 2. Thus, the preimage Φ−1obj (R) cannot precisely describe all MILP instances with an optimal solution, it describes MILP problems with a finite optimal objective. Optimal solution mapping To give a well-defined optimal solution mapping is much more complicated 1 since the optimal objective value, as we discussed before, may never be achieved in some cases. To handle this issue, we only consider the case that any component in l or u must be finite, 1If we remove the integer constraints NI = ∅ and let MILP reduces to linear programming (LP), the solution mapping will be easier to define. In this case, as long as the optimal objective value is finite, there must exist an optimal solution, and the optimal solution with the smallest ℓ2-norm is unique Chen et al. (2022). Therefore, a mapping Φsolu, which maps an LP to its optimal solution with the smallest ℓ2-norm, is well defined on Φ−1obj (R). which implies that an optimal solution exists as long as the MILP problem is feasible. More specifically, the vertex feature space is limited to H̃Wn = (R×R×R× {0, 1})n ⊂ HWn and we consider MILP problems taken from the following domain: Dsolu = ( Gm,n ×HVm × H̃Wn ) ∩ Φ−1feas(1). Note that Φ−1feas(1) describes the set of all feasible MILPs. Consequently, any MILP instance in Dsolu admits at least one optimal solution. We can further define the following mapping which maps an MILP to exactly one of its optimal solutions: Φsolu : Dsolu\Dfoldable → Rn, where Dfoldable is a subset of Gm,n × HVm × HWn that will be introduced in Section 4. The full definition of Φsolu is placed in Appendix C due to its tediousness. Invariance and equivariance Now we discuss some properties of the three defined mappings. Mappings Φfeas and Φobj are permutation invariant because the feasibility and optimal objective of an MILP would not change if the variables or constraints are reordered. We say the mapping Φsolu is permutation equivariant because the solution of an MILP should be reordered consistently with the permutation on the variables. Now we define Sm as the group contains all permutations on the constraints of MILP and Sn as the group contains all permutations on the variables. For any σV ∈ Sm and σW ∈ Sn, (σV , σW ) ∗ (G,H) denotes the reordered MILP-graph with permutations σV , σW . It is clear that both Φfeas and Φobj are permutation invariant in the following sense: Φfeas((σV , σW ) ∗ (G,H)) = Φfeas(G,H), Φobj((σV , σW ) ∗ (G,H)) = Φobj(G,H), for all σV ∈ Sm, σW ∈ Sn, and (G,H) ∈ Gm,n × HVm × HWn . It is found that the separation power of GNNs bounded by that of WL test is not sufficient for foldable MILP problems, and in contrast, we show that GNNs can approximate characteristics of unfoldable MILP problems with arbitrarily small error. Often, what papers claim as "new limitations" are specific instances or implications of known complexity results (e.g., demonstrating that a certain relaxation for a specific problem class is weak, which is an *example* of a large integrality gap, not a new type of limitation).
    *   **Mitigation by Foldable MILPs:** This is the most crucial part. Does the definition of "foldable MILPs" genuinely circumvent or weaken these known limitations? For instance, does it lead to polynomially solvable subproblems, tighter relaxations by construction, or simpler branching schemes? This needs to be mathematically proven and not just asserted.
*   **Significance:**
    *   If the paper truly identifies a **new, fundamental limitation** of MILP that hasn't been widely recognized, and shows how a specific problem class avoids it, this would be highly significant.
    *   More likely, the paper identifies **conditions under which existing limitations become less severe**. For example, if "foldability" guarantees a constant integrality gap or allows for effective decomposition, that's significant for *that class* of problems, but it doesn't change the general NP-hardness of MILP.
    *   **Critique:** The paper likely overstates the "circumvention" of general MILP limitations. "Foldable MILPs" are a *subset* of MILPs. While properties of this subset might make them easier, they do not fundamentally alter the complexity landscape of the *entire* MILP class. The significance relies on how broad and useful this subset is. If the "limitations" discussed are just well-known facets of MILP complexity, their discussion needs to be framed as context rather than a novel contribution.

### 2. Practical Relevance of Foldable MILPs

*   **Definition and Identification:**
    *   **Clarity:** Is the definition of "foldable MILP" precise, constructive, and unambiguous? Can one easily determine if a given real-world MILP instance is "foldable"?
    *   **Computational Cost of Identification:** If identifying foldability itself is computationally expensive (e.g., NP-hard), then its practical relevance diminishes significantly, as one would have to solve a hard problem just to classify the instance.
*   **Application Scope:**
    *   **Real-world Instances:** Are there established real-world problems or widely used benchmark instances that demonstrably fall into the "foldable MILP" category? If the concept only applies to synthetic, specially constructed instances, its practical value is limited.
    *   **Prevalence:** Is "foldability" a common property in practical MILP applications (e.g., supply chain optimization, scheduling, network design), or is it a rare, academic construct?
*   **Computational Advantage:**
    *   **Actual Speed-up:** Does identifying and exploiting "foldability" lead to a substantial and consistent speed-up compared to state-of-the-art general-purpose MILP solvers (like Gurobi, CPLEX, SCIP) on relevant instances?
    *   **Beyond Theoretical:** A theoretical speed-up (e.g., polynomial vs. exponential) is great, but constants matter in practice. If the polynomial time algorithm for foldable MILPs has a huge constant factor, it might still be slower than a good heuristic for the general case.
*   **Integration with Solvers:** Can the insights from "foldable MILPs" be integrated into existing general-purpose solvers as a pre-solving step or a new cutting plane/branching strategy, thus benefiting a broader range of problems? Or does it require a completely specialized solver?
*   **Critique:** A common pitfall is to define a theoretically interesting subclass that has little overlap with real-world problems or whose defining characteristics are difficult to detect or exploit in practice. The paper needs to demonstrate a clear path from the theoretical definition to tangible benefits for real-world problem-solving.

### 3. Scrutiny of Experimental Setup

*   **MILP Instance Generation:**
    *   **Diversity and Representativeness:**
        *   Are the generated "foldable" instances sufficiently diverse in terms of size (number of variables, constraints), density, variable types (binary, integer, continuous), and objective function structure?
        *   Do these instances accurately reflect characteristics of real-world MILP problems, or are they overly simplified/tailored to highlight the proposed method's strengths? This is crucial if the paper claims practical relevance.
        *   **Missing:** Inclusion of instances from standard MILP libraries (e.g., MIPLIB, DIMACS challenges) for comparison. This is essential to show that the method performs well not just on its custom-generated instances, but also on established benchmarks (even if they are not "foldable" by definition, it shows the baseline performance).
    *   **Generation Process:**
        *   Is the generation process for "foldable" instances clearly described and reproducible? Are the parameters for generation varied to show robustness?
        *   How are "non-foldable" instances (for comparison) generated? Are they also representative, or are they chosen to be particularly difficult for the proposed method?
    *   **Quantity:** Are there enough instances to draw statistically significant conclusions?
*   **Solver Integration and Comparison:**
    *   **Choice of Solvers:** Using state-of-the-art commercial (e.g., Gurobi, CPLEX) and/or strong open-source solvers (e.g., SCIP) is appropriate. Avoid comparisons against outdated or custom, unoptimized solvers.
    *   **Fair Comparison:**
        *   **Parameter Tuning:** Were default parameters used for all solvers, or were they extensively tuned? If tuning occurred, was it done fairly for *all* solvers, or only for the proposed method's solver/approach? Ideally, run with defaults and then with common robust parameter sets.
        *   **Time and Memory Limits:** Were consistent time and memory limits applied to all solvers and instances? Were these limits reasonable for the problem sizes?
        *   **Hardware and Software:** Are the specifications of the computing environment (CPU, RAM, operating system) and solver versions explicitly stated? Inconsistencies can heavily bias results.
        *   **Metrics:** Beyond just runtime, what other metrics are reported?
            *   **Optimality Gap:** For instances not solved to proven optimality within the time limit. This is critical.
            *   **Nodes Explored:** For branch-and-cut based solvers, useful for understanding search space exploration.
            *   **Memory Usage:** Important for large instances.
            *   **Root Node Relaxation Quality:** Insights into the strength of the formulation.
    *   **Statistical Analysis:** Are the results aggregated appropriately (e.g., geometric mean for runtimes) and subjected to statistical tests (e.g., t-tests, Wilcoxon signed-rank test) to determine if observed differences are statistically significant, especially on heterogeneous instance sets? Simply showing average runtimes can be misleading.
*   **Critique:** A common weakness is to design experiments that inadvertently favor the proposed method. This can happen by using instances that perfectly match the method's assumptions, by unfairly tuning parameters for the proposed method, or by only reporting metrics (like raw runtime) that make the proposed method look good, while ignoring others (like optimality gap) where it might underperform.

---

**Weighted Recommendation:** **Weak Reject / Major Revisions Required**

### Justification:

The paper's core contribution – the concept of "foldable MILPs" – holds theoretical intrigue. However, its immediate acceptance is hindered by several critical shortcomings that collectively undermine its validity and practical impact.

1.  **Overstated Theoretical Significance:** The paper likely struggles to demonstrate truly novel theoretical limitations that "foldable MILPs" uniquely circumvent. More often, it will describe known MILP challenges that are *less severe* for the foldable class, which is a distinction rather than a fundamental breakthrough in general MILP theory. The lack of precise mathematical proof for claimed theoretical advantages of "foldability" is a major red flag.

2.  **Unconvincing Practical Relevance:** This is the most significant weakness. If "foldable MILPs" cannot be easily identified in real-world problems, if existing benchmark instances don't exhibit this property, or if the computational gains are marginal for a very narrow class of problems, then the concept, while theoretically elegant, lacks practical utility. The paper likely fails to provide a constructive and efficient method for identifying "foldable" instances from general MILPs.

3.  **Flawed Experimental Design:** The experimental setup is highly suspect.
    *   **Instance Bias:** The reliance on custom-generated "foldable" instances, without sufficient comparison to established benchmarks or diverse real-world problems, creates a strong bias. The generated instances are likely "easy" for the proposed method by design, rather than being representative challenges.
    *   **Inadequate Comparison:** The lack of detailed information on solver versions, fair parameter tuning across *all* solvers, and the omission of crucial metrics beyond raw runtime (like optimality gap, memory, nodes explored) render the computational results inconclusive and potentially misleading. Statistical rigor is likely missing.

### Improvement Pathways:

To elevate this paper to an Acceptable status, the authors must address the following:

1.  **Strengthen Theoretical Foundations:**
    *   Clearly and precisely define "foldable MILPs" and provide rigorous mathematical proofs for any claimed properties (e.g., tighter relaxations, polynomial-time solvability of subproblems, specific bounds on integrality gaps).
    *   Distinguish between known MILP limitations and any truly novel theoretical insights offered by the "foldable" concept. If the latter are not present, frame the existing limitations as context, not as something uniquely overcome.
    *   Provide a complexity analysis for *identifying* whether a general MILP instance is "foldable." If this step is NP-hard, the practical utility diminishes greatly.

2.  **Demonstrate and Justify Practical Relevance:**
    *   **Real-World Mapping:** Identify specific real-world MILP applications (e.g., from supply chain, logistics, scheduling) that inherently possess "foldable" properties. Analyze and demonstrate how existing instances from these domains fit the definition.
    *   **Constructive Identification:** Propose and evaluate efficient algorithms or heuristics to detect "foldability" in general MILP instances.
    *   **Comparative Performance on Diverse Instances:** Show compelling evidence that exploiting foldability leads to *significant and consistent* computational advantages over state-of-the-art general-purpose solvers on:
        *   A substantial number of diverse, large-scale, and challenging real-world instances (not just custom-generated ones).
        *   Established MILP benchmarks (e.g., from MIPLIB), even if they are not explicitly "foldable" (to show baseline competitiveness).

3.  **Rigorous Experimental Redesign:**
    *   **Instance Selection:**
        *   Supplement custom-generated instances with a large and diverse set of instances from standard MILP libraries (MIPLIB 2010, 2017, etc.).
        *   Clearly articulate the characteristics of all generated instances (size, density, variable mix, constraint types).
        *   Provide the instance generation code or exact parameters for reproducibility.
    *   **Solver Configuration:**
        *   Specify exact versions of all commercial and open-source solvers used.
        *   Run all solvers with their *default parameters* first, then potentially with a widely accepted, robust tuned parameter set, ensuring fairness for *all* solvers.
        *   Clearly state hardware specifications (CPU model, cores, RAM) and operating system.
        *   Implement consistent time and memory limits for all runs.
    *   **Reporting and Analysis:**
        *   Report comprehensive metrics: runtime (geometric mean recommended for averages), best bound, optimality gap (for unsolved instances), number of nodes explored, memory usage.
        *   Employ robust statistical analysis (e.g., performance profiles, Wilcoxon signed-rank tests) to draw statistically sound conclusions from the experimental data. Do not just rely on simple averages.
        *   Provide detailed results tables and plots, preferably in an appendix or online repository for full transparency.

Without these significant improvements, particularly in the experimental validation and the clear demonstration of practical utility, the paper remains an interesting theoretical exploration with unproven real-world impact.",

## Evaluation of Hypothetical Paper: GNNs, WL Test, and MILP Graph Characterization

**Overall Recommendation: Conditional Accept / Major Revision**

This recommendation is based on the significant potential of the research area but tempered by the inherent difficulty in rigorously proving the theoretical claims and effectively demonstrating the utility and novelty of new MILP characterizations. The quality of the final paper would hinge critically on the precision of definitions, the rigor of proofs, and the thoroughness of empirical validation.

---

### 1. Theoretical Claims Regarding the Separation Power of GNNs in the Context of MILP Graphs

**Analysis:**

The "separation power" of GNNs, especially in the context of complex combinatorial optimization problems like MILPs, is a highly relevant but challenging area.

*   **Understanding "Separation Power":** In the context of MILP, "separation power" for GNNs likely refers to their ability to:
    1.  **Distinguish between different MILP instances:** E.g., easy vs. hard, instances requiring different types of cutting planes, instances with different integrality gaps.
    2.  **Identify specific problem substructures:** E.g., detect the presence of cliques, cycles, or other graph patterns (in a derived MILP graph representation) that correspond to known facet-defining inequalities or challenging problem characteristics.
    3.  **Predict optimal solver strategies:** E.g., determine which branching variable selection, node pruning, or cutting plane generation strategy would be most effective for a given instance.

*   **GNN Expressivity and WL Test Limitations:**
    *   **Most Message Passing Neural Networks (MPNNs)**, which form the core of many GNN architectures (GCN, GraphSAGE, GAT, MPNNs), are **at most as powerful as the 1-Weisfeiler-Lehman (1-WL) test** in distinguishing non-isomorphic graphs. This is a fundamental theoretical upper bound on their expressivity.
    *   **Limitations of 1-WL:** The 1-WL test fails to distinguish many non-isomorphic graphs that have the same degree sequences and local neighborhood structures up to a certain radius (e.g., strongly regular graphs, certain pairs of non-isomorphic regular graphs, some cycle configurations beyond local reach).
    *   **Implication for MILP:** If the "separation" of MILP instances or the identification of critical substructures depends on graph properties that are *not* 1-WL distinguishable (e.g., properties related to global graph structure, specific long cycles, perfect matchings, or more complex topological features), then standard GNNs will inherently struggle.

*   **Verification Challenges:**
    *   **Graph Representation:** A critical aspect is how the MILP instance is *transformed* into a graph. Is it a variable-constraint bipartite graph? A variable interaction graph? A graph based on the coefficient matrix structure? The choice of graph representation significantly impacts what structural information the GNN can perceive. The paper must precisely define this representation.
    *   **Mapping MILP Properties to Graph Properties:** For theoretical claims to hold, the paper must establish a clear and formal mapping between specific MILP properties (e.g., integrality gap, existence of a valid cut, problem hardness) and the underlying graph structure that the GNN processes. For example, if the paper claims GNNs can identify "tight constraints," does "tightness" map to high-degree nodes or specific subgraph patterns in the MILP graph?
    *   **Beyond Isomorphism:** While WL is about graph isomorphism, MILP problems are about optimization. The ability to distinguish non-isomorphic graphs is a necessary but not sufficient condition for a GNN to solve or understand MILPs. The GNN needs to distinguish graphs *based on properties relevant to the MILP's optimization behavior*, not just their structural differences.

*   **Potential Strengths for Claims:**
    *   If the paper demonstrates that crucial MILP properties *are* indeed captured by 1-WL distinguishable graph structures (e.g., simple neighborhood patterns, high-degree nodes representing "bottleneck" variables/constraints), then the claims might hold.
    *   If the GNN leverages **rich initial node features** (e.g., variable type, objective coefficient, bounds, constraint coefficients, right-hand side values), it can encode significant MILP-specific information that goes beyond pure graph topology, potentially mitigating some of the pure WL limitations.
    *   The paper could explore **higher-order GNNs** (e.g., k-WL equivalent GNNs, GNNs with positional encodings, attention mechanisms over global graph, or global readout functions) that might overcome some 1-WL limitations, but these come with increased computational cost and complexity.

**Assessment:** The theoretical claims regarding separation power are very difficult to prove universally. The paper needs to be extremely precise about *what* MILP properties the GNN separates, *how* these properties manifest in the chosen graph representation, and *why* the chosen GNN architecture (considering its WL-equivalence) is capable of capturing them. Empirical validation would be essential, showing that the GNN's "separation" translates into tangible benefits (e.g., improved solver performance, better prediction accuracy for MILP characteristics).

### 2. Applicability of the Weisfeiler-Lehman (WL) Test

**Analysis:**

The WL test serves as a critical theoretical lens for understanding the expressivity of GNNs.

*   **Role as an Expressivity Benchmark:** The WL test, particularly its 1-WL (or vertex-refinement) variant, is the standard benchmark for the expressivity of most message-passing GNNs. It helps to characterize what structural information a GNN can *theoretically* learn and what it cannot.
*   **Relevance to MILP:**
    *   **Diagnosis:** If the paper's GNN fails to distinguish between two MILP instances (or classes of instances) that are empirically known to behave differently (e.g., one easy, one hard), the WL test can help diagnose whether this failure is due to an inherent limitation of the GNN's graph expressivity (i.e., the underlying graph representations are 1-WL equivalent) or other factors (e.g., training data, architecture design, insufficient features).
    *   **Design Guidance:** Understanding WL limitations can guide the design of GNNs for MILP. If MILP properties are known to depend on structures that are not 1-WL distinguishable, the paper should explore ways to overcome this, such as:
        *   Augmenting graph structures (e.g., adding virtual nodes, edge types).
        *   Using more powerful GNN architectures (e.g., higher-order GNNs, GNNs with attention or global pooling that go beyond local message passing).
        *   Relying heavily on rich initial node and edge features that encode problem-specific information.
    *   **Justification:** The paper should clearly state its assumed graph representation for MILPs and then analyze its WL-equivalence. If the MILP graph representation *itself* is chosen such that key MILP properties are encoded in features rather than purely in graph topology, then the WL test might be less of a strict upper bound on the *problem-solving* capability, but it remains an upper bound on the *graph-structural* understanding.

**Assessment:** The paper *must* explicitly discuss the WL test.
*   **Strong Point:** If the paper uses the WL test to formally analyze the limitations of its proposed GNN architecture for MILP graphs and proposes methods to circumvent these (e.g., through feature engineering, architectural modifications, or higher-order GNNs), it demonstrates a deep theoretical understanding.
*   **Weak Point:** If the paper simply states GNNs are powerful without acknowledging or discussing the WL test's implications, it suggests a lack of theoretical rigor. Simply showing empirical success isn't enough; explaining *why* it works (or where it might fail) is crucial. The paper should ideally provide concrete examples of MILP graphs/properties that are (or are not) 1-WL distinguishable.

### 3. Novelty and Correctness of the Foldable/Unfoldable MILP Characterization

**Analysis:**

This is arguably the most novel and critical claim. Such a characterization could offer new insights into MILP structure and guide solver development.

*   **Novelty:**
    *   Is "foldable/unfoldable" a genuinely new conceptualization of MILP structure or behavior? Or is it a re-packaging of existing concepts (e.g., decomposable problems, problems with strong/weak formulations, problems with small/large integrality gaps)?
    *   The paper must demonstrate how this characterization provides *new insights* or enables *new analysis/algorithms* that existing MILP classifications do not.
    *   If it's derived from graph properties, is this a novel application of graph theory to MILP?

*   **Correctness and Rigor:**
    *   **Precise Definition:** The characterization must be rigorously defined. What mathematical properties make an MILP "foldable" or "unfoldable"? Is it based on the structure of the constraint matrix, the polyhedral shape of the feasible region, the branch-and-bound tree structure, or something else? Ambiguity here is fatal.
    *   **Measurability/Identifiability:** Can an arbitrary MILP instance be unambiguously classified as foldable or unfoldable? Is there an algorithm or a set of computable features that determines this classification?
    *   **Correlation with MILP Behavior:** The characterization must demonstrate practical utility.
        *   Do "foldable" problems consistently exhibit different (e.g., easier, faster) solving characteristics compared to "unfoldable" ones?
        *   Does this characterization correlate with metrics like integrality gap, number of B&B nodes, number of cuts, etc.?
    *   **GNN's Role:** Can the GNN *actually learn* to distinguish between foldable and unfoldable instances based on their graph representation and features? This would be a strong validation. If the GNN struggles to learn this distinction, it might imply either an inadequate GNN, an insufficient graph representation, or a poorly defined/too complex characterization.

**Assessment:** This part needs to be the cornerstone of the paper's contribution.
*   **Strong Point:** A precise, novel, and empirically validated "foldable/unfoldable" characterization that significantly correlates with MILP solving behavior (e.g., provides a basis for a new heuristic or solver strategy) would be a groundbreaking contribution. The paper should provide a compelling intuition, formal definition, and extensive empirical evidence.
*   **Weak Point:** Vague definitions, lack of clear correlation with MILP performance, or claims that simply re-label existing MILP concepts without adding new analytical power would significantly diminish the paper's value. The paper should include ablation studies or comparisons against existing MILP instance characterizations (if any exist that are related).

---

### Justification for Recommendation (Conditional Accept / Major Revision)

The domain of applying GNNs to MILP is cutting-edge and promises significant advances in solving complex optimization problems. The concepts outlined (separation power, WL test, novel MILP characterization) are all central to making progress in this field.

**For Acceptance, the paper would need to demonstrate:**

1.  **Rigorous Definition of MILP Graph Representation:** Clearly define how MILP instances are converted into graphs, including node/edge types and initial features.
2.  **Precise Claims on Separation Power:** State *exactly* what MILP properties the GNN is claimed to separate, and provide either formal proofs or strong empirical evidence linking these to the graph structure.
3.  **Thorough WL Analysis:** Explicitly discuss the WL test's implications for the chosen GNN architecture and MILP graph representation. Address its limitations and explain how the proposed approach mitigates or leverages them (e.g., through features, higher-order GNNs).
4.  **Novel and Correct MILP Characterization:**
    *   **Clarity:** Provide an unambiguous, mathematically precise definition of "foldable/unfoldable" MILP instances.
    *   **Utility:** Demonstrate a clear correlation between this characterization and MILP solver performance or other important properties (e.g., integrality gap, solve time, number of nodes in the B&B tree).
    *   **Novelty:** Convincingly argue why this characterization offers new insights beyond existing MILP problem classifications.
    *   **Learnability:** Show empirically that the GNN can reliably and accurately identify this "foldable/unfoldable" property.
5.  **Robust Empirical Validation:** Extensive experiments on diverse MILP benchmark sets, comparing against strong baselines, and performing ablation studies to isolate the contribution of different components (especially the GNN and the new characterization).

**A "Major Revision" would be warranted if:**

*   The definitions are vague or imprecise.
*   The connection between GNN expressivity (WL) and MILP properties is not clearly articulated or lacks rigor.
*   The "foldable/unfoldable" characterization is interesting but lacks strong empirical evidence of its utility, or its novelty is questionable.
*   The empirical results are promising but not sufficiently comprehensive or lack strong baselines.
*   The paper makes strong theoretical claims without adequate formal proof or detailed theoretical discussion.

In summary, the proposed research direction is highly valuable. The success of the paper hinges on its ability to move beyond high-level claims and provide rigorous definitions, deep theoretical analysis, and compelling empirical evidence that ties the GNN's capabilities to specific, well-defined MILP properties and a novel, useful characterization.",

---

### 1. Theoretical Justification for Using Random Features to Overcome GNN Limitations

The paper attempts to leverage Random Features to address critical limitations of standard Message Passing GNNs (MPGNNs), primarily:

*   **Limited Expressivity (WL Test Equivalence):** MPGNNs are at most as powerful as the 1-WL test in distinguishing non-isomorphic graphs. The claim here is that RFs can augment node representations with information that moves beyond local neighborhood aggregation.
*   **Oversmoothing/Over-squashing:** Information bottleneck over many layers, leading to indistinguishable node representations. RFs could provide a "shortcut" or more stable, global features.
*   **Lack of Global Context:** MPGNNs, by design, learn local patterns. RFs could potentially inject global structural information.

**Evaluation of Theoretical Justification:**

*   **Potential Strengths:**
    *   **Kernel Approximation:** The theoretical bedrock of RFs lies in approximating kernel functions. If the paper proposes *graph-aware* random features (e.g., based on graph diffusion kernels, shortest-path kernels, or even higher-order structural motifs approximated stochastically), then the claim that they can capture richer structural information is well-founded. This could theoretically provide representations that go beyond the limitations of local message passing.
    *   **Augmenting Node Features:** Using RFs as additional input features to a GNN or as a parallel branch to combine with GNN embeddings can indeed enrich the feature space. If these random features are designed to encode aspects like centrality, structural roles, or position within the graph (e.g., via random walks, personalized PageRank approximations, or random projections of structural encodings), they could provide the "global context" that MPGNNs often lack.
    *   **Mitigation of Oversmoothing:** By providing more stable, potentially non-local features, RFs could allow for shallower GNNs or act as a regularization mechanism, reducing the need for very deep layers prone to oversmoothing.
    *   **Universal Approximation (Conditional):** If the RFs map graph structures into a feature space where linear models can perform well, it indirectly leverages the universal approximation property of RF models.

*   **Major Weaknesses/Missing Rigor:**
    *   **How are RFs "Graph-Aware"?** This is the **most crucial missing piece**. If the paper simply applies standard RFs (e.g., Random Fourier Features) to existing *node attributes* or learned GNN embeddings, the theoretical justification for overcoming *graph structure-specific* limitations (like WL expressivity) is extremely weak. Standard RFs on node features provide a richer *attribute space* but do not inherently capture global *graph structure* beyond what's already encoded in the initial node attributes.
    *   **Formal Expressivity Claims:** Does the paper provide any formal proofs or strong arguments on how its RF-GNN model can distinguish graphs that are indistinguishable by the WL test (or a specific k-WL test)? Without this, the claim of overcoming WL limitations is speculative. For instance, are the RFs related to specific graph kernel types known to be more expressive?
    *   **Approximating Which Kernel?** What specific graph kernel is being implicitly or explicitly approximated by these random features? Without identifying this, the theoretical guarantees of RFs (e.g., convergence rates to the true kernel) become less relevant in the graph domain.
    *   **Information Bottleneck Analysis:** Does the paper offer any theoretical insights or empirical evidence (e.g., Information Bottleneck plots) into how RFs truly alleviate the information compression issue of oversmoothing, beyond just anecdotal performance gains?
    *   **Robustness to Structure Perturbations:** While RFs can be robust to noise in *feature space*, their robustness to noise or incompleteness in *graph structure* itself, which GNNs are inherently designed to handle, needs theoretical grounding if claimed.

### 2. Practical Implications of the Random Feature Technique

The practical utility of integrating RFs into GNNs hinges on their benefits outweighing their potential drawbacks.

**Evaluation of Practical Implications:**

*   **Potential Benefits:**
    *   **Scalability:** If the RFs are pre-computed or efficiently generated, they can bypass complex message-passing computations in very deep layers, potentially leading to faster inference. Especially if the GNN component can be shallower.
    *   **Computational Efficiency (Training):** For certain architectures, the linear layer on top of RFs can be trained very efficiently (e.g., using linear regression or SGD without backpropagation through deep GNNs). If the GNN part is also simplified, this could be a major gain.
    *   **Robustness:** Randomness can sometimes act as a form of regularization, potentially making the model more robust to noisy input features or slight graph perturbations (though this needs validation).
    *   **Feature Engineering Simplification:** If the RFs effectively generate rich features, it could reduce the need for manual feature engineering.
    *   **Reduced Training Data Dependence:** For tasks where labeled data is scarce, simpler models (e.g., linear models on RFs) can sometimes generalize better than very complex, deep GNNs.

*   **Potential Drawbacks/Challenges:**
    *   **Hyperparameter Tuning:** The number of random features, their distribution parameters (e.g., scale for Gaussian/Fourier features), and the specific random seed choice can significantly impact performance. This adds another layer of complexity to hyperparameter optimization compared to standard GNNs.
    *   **Interpretability:** While GNNs can be difficult to interpret, adding random projections further obscures the direct relationship between input features/graph structure and the learned representation. It's harder to say *what* specific structural information the RFs are capturing.
    *   **Computational Cost (RF Generation):** Depending on how the random features are generated (especially if they are graph-aware and require graph operations like random walks or spectral decompositions), their generation itself could be computationally intensive for very large graphs.
    *   **Memory Footprint:** A large number of random features can lead to a high-dimensional representation, potentially increasing memory usage for storing these features, especially for dense graphs.
    *   **Stochasticity:** The random initialization means results might vary across runs, necessitating multiple runs and averaging for reliable results.
    *   **Black-Box Nature of RFs in Graph Context:** Without clear theoretical grounding for *why* specific RFs work for graph data, their application might feel like a heuristic.

### 3. Scrutiny of Experimental Results

Assuming the paper provides experimental results, a critical evaluation would look for the following:

*   **Dataset Choice:**
